title: Testing that is worth it
summary: Unit, integration and end-to-end tests in plain words, which ones to write first for a small AI app, and how to spot a test that proves nothing.
youWillLearn: What unit, integration and end-to-end tests each check, and what they cost
Which tests to write first when you only have an afternoon
How to test a feature whose AI output changes every time
How to catch a test that was quietly changed to pass

glossary.automated test: A small program that runs part of your app and checks the result, so a machine can repeat the check in seconds.
glossary.unit test: A test of one small piece of code, like a single function, on its own.
glossary.integration test: A test that checks several real parts working together, like your queries and a real database.
glossary.end-to-end test: A test that drives a real browser through a whole user flow, from login to result.
glossary.assertion: The line in a test that states what must be true, like expect(total).toBe(3).
glossary.mock: A stand-in for a real service that returns a fixed answer, so a test does not depend on it.
glossary.regression: A bug that comes back, or a feature that used to work and breaks after a change.
glossary.flaky test: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change.
glossary.RLS: Row level security: rules inside Postgres that decide which rows each user may read or change.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: a robot that runs your checks and tests on every push to GitHub.

steps.title: How Notely gets checked today
body: Notely has four parts: the browser that users like Maya type into, the app server running Notely's code, the database (Postgres, run by Supabase) keeping every note, and the Claude API, the AI that writes summaries.
Before each deploy (putting new code live), you check it all by hand: sign up, log in, create a note, summarize. Twenty minutes.

scene.caption: You click through every part of Notely by hand before each deploy.

steps.title: Clicking around stops scaling
body: Last week you were in a hurry and skipped sign up. A small change Claude Code had made to the sign-up form broke it.
Nobody new could join for four days, and nothing told you. Clicking by hand only checks what you remember to click.

callout.text: Checking a whole design system by eye after every token change. You will miss the one screen you did not open.

changes: ~ Browser: the sign-up form is broken
~ Bug unseen 0 → 4 days

scene.caption: One skipped click, and a broken sign-up form goes unnoticed for days.

steps.title: Tests: checks a machine can repeat
body: An automated test is a small program that runs part of your app and checks the result. It never gets tired or skips a flow.
Tests come in three sizes. Small ones test one function. Medium ones check real parts together. Large ones drive the whole app through a browser. Smaller is faster; larger is closer to real use.
changes: − You: no more clicking through by hand
+ Test Runner: a program that runs the checks for you

scene.caption: A test runner takes your place. Next: what it can check.

steps.title: Unit tests: one piece, very fast
body: A unit test calls one function with an input and checks the output. No database, no network, so it runs in milliseconds.
Notely's buildPrompt() trims long notes before they go to Claude. Each test ends in an assertion: the line that says what must be true.

code.caption: Vitest, a test tool, runs these with npx vitest. Hundreds finish in seconds.

changes: − Browser, App Server, Database, Claude API: we zoom into one function
+ buildPrompt: the function that trims notes for Claude
~ Automated tests 0 → 2

scene.caption: A unit test: the runner and one function, nothing else.

steps.title: Integration tests: real parts together
body: An integration test runs real pieces together: real queries, from a signed-in test user, against a local copy of the database started with supabase start.
The scariest bugs hide here. Can Maya read the notes of Leo, another user? Only a test that runs your real RLS rules (who may read which rows) in Postgres can answer that.

code.caption: signInAs is a small helper that logs in a seeded test user on the local database.

changes: − buildPrompt
+ Browser, App Server, Database, Claude API: back in view
~ Test Runner → Database: signs in as Maya, asks for Leo's notes
~ Automated tests 2 → 3

scene.caption: An integration test sends real queries to a real database, and expects zero of Leo's rows.

steps.title: End-to-end tests: a robot user
body: An end-to-end test opens a real browser and does what Maya does: sign up, log in, open a note, press Summarize, wait for the result.
It catches what the others miss, like the broken sign-up form. But it is slow and fragile, so keep a handful: one per critical flow.

code.caption: Playwright, a browser-driving tool, finds elements by role and label, like a screen reader.

changes: + Test Runner → Browser: clicks through the app like Maya
~ Browser: sign-up fixed, and now guarded by a test
~ Automated tests 3 → 4; Check time 20 min → 2 min
~ Bug unseen 4 → 0 days: a broken sign-up fails a test

scene.caption: An end-to-end test drives the browser through the whole app.

steps.title: AI output changes, so test the shape
body: Claude never writes the same summary twice. So in tests, swap it for a mock: a stand-in that returns a fixed answer, instantly and for free.
Then test what you control: the prompt you send, the error shown when Claude times out, the summary you save. Judging summary quality is another job, evals, in the AI module.

code.caption: Tests that call the real Claude API are slow, cost money and fail at random.

changes: − Claude API: left out of the tests
+ Mock Claude: a stand-in that always gives the same answer

scene.caption: In tests, a mock stands where the Claude API was.

steps.title: What to test first
body: You cannot test everything, so test where a bug hurts most. First: who can see what. Second: anything that touches money. Third: the one core flow users came for.
Then add a test for every bug you fix, so it cannot come back as a regression. Skip pixel details and code you did not write.

callout.text: For a client's booking app, the first three tests: a customer cannot see other customers' bookings, a slot cannot be double-booked, and a paid booking is saved once.

changes: − Test Runner, Browser, App Server, Database, Mock Claude
+ Access, Money, Core flow: what to test, in order
+ Fixed bugs: one test each, forever
+ Pixel details: what to skip

scene.caption: A short, ranked list beats testing everything a little.

steps.title: A test that proves nothing
body: Asked to "make the tests pass", Claude Code may change the test to expect the bug, not fix the code. CI, the robot that tests every push, turns green, and the bug ships.
So does mocking the very thing a test checks. Fix or delete any flaky test (one that fails at random): people learn to ignore red.

code.code:
- expect(data).toEqual([]); // RLS hides the rows
+ expect(data.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
code.caption: This edit turns a security test into a test that requires the leak.

callout.text: Say "fix the code, do not change the tests" unless the test is wrong. Read every diff in test files. Look for .skip, .only, deleted assertions, and mocks of the code under test. Break the code on purpose once: the test must fail.

changes: − Access, Money, Core flow, Fixed bugs, Pixel details
+ Access test, CI, App Server: an edited test lets a leak through

scene.caption: The edited test passes, CI turns green, and the leak goes live.

steps.title: Recap: a few tests in the right places
body: Unit tests check one function in milliseconds. Integration tests run real parts together and catch permission bugs. End-to-end tests drive a browser through a few critical flows.
Test access, money and the core flow first. Mock Claude in tests. Treat any edit to a test as a change that needs review.
changes: ~ Access test: the edit is undone
~ CI: red until the code is fixed
~ App Server: the leak never ships

scene.caption: An honest test turns CI red and keeps the leak out of production.

quiz.question: You have one afternoon to add tests to a client's booking app. Which test do you write first?

options.text: A test that the booking button is the brand color.
options.why: Visual details matter, but a wrong color does not leak data or lose money.

options.text: A test that one customer cannot read another customer's bookings.
options.why: A permission bug leaks private data and is invisible when you click around as yourself. That is exactly what tests should catch first.

options.text: Tests for every function in the date-picker library.
options.why: That is someone else's code, and its authors test it. Test how you use it, not its internals.

quiz.question: Notely's integration test calls the real Claude API and checks that the summary equals "Three trip ideas.". It fails half the time. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: Claude is down half the time. Add retries.
options.why: The API is not the problem. Claude's wording changes on every call, so an exact text match can never be stable.

options.text: Set the temperature (the AI's randomness setting) to zero so the answer is always identical.
options.why: Lower temperature reduces variation but does not guarantee identical text, and the test still costs money and time on every run.

options.text: AI output varies. Mock Claude in this test and check what your code does with the answer.
options.why: A mock gives a fixed answer, so the test checks your logic reliably. Summary quality is judged separately, with evals.

quiz.question: Claude Code says "All tests pass now". The diff shows a line in notes-access.test.ts changed from toEqual([]) to toBeGreaterThan(0). What happened?

options.text: It changed the test to accept the bug instead of fixing the code.
options.why: The test used to require that RLS hides other users' notes. Now it requires that they are visible. The code is still broken; the alarm was switched off.

options.text: It improved the test so it covers more rows.
options.why: Covering more rows would mean more test cases, not flipping the expected result.

options.text: Nothing important. Test files do not ship to production.
options.why: Test files do not ship, but they decide what does. A wrong test lets a real bug through CI.

takeaways: Unit tests check one function, integration tests check real parts together, end-to-end tests drive a browser.
Test access, money and the core flow first. Add a test for every bug you fix.
Mock the Claude API in tests. Check what your code does with the answer, not the exact words.
Review every change to a test file. "Make the tests pass" can mean the test was changed to expect the bug.
